content.intro: Learn installing django through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Installing Django matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines installing django as part of development environment and project setup. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Installing Django with pip; Installing a specific compatible release; Verifying the installed version; Understanding Python packages and dependencies; Avoiding installation into the wrong environment. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Installing Django with pip
items.text: Install Django using the active interpreter (`python -m pip install ...`) so pip cannot silently target another Python installation. Pin a reviewed compatible patch release for reproducible deployments.

items.title: Installing a specific compatible release
items.text: Installing a specific compatible release should be planned for the actual hosting topology: configuration, permissions, resource limits, observability, rollback/recovery and a testable operating procedure all matter.

items.title: Verifying the installed version
items.text: Use `python -m django --version` and compare it with the environment and release notes used by the project. The Python command and Django package should come from the same virtual environment.

items.title: Understanding Python packages and dependencies
items.text: For Understanding Python packages and dependencies, identify the Django component responsible, the inputs and outputs it owns, and the boundary conditions that matter. Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Installing Django
content_blocks.code:
python -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip --version
python -m django --version
content_blocks.expected_output: The commands run package/version checks inside the activated environment.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open a local project using the documented Django 6.1-compatible Python environment. If this snippet depends on model names, URL configuration, settings, or an optional package, add those prerequisites before running it. Otherwise inspect it as a static example. CodeLeaf browser preview does not execute Django/Python server code.
content_blocks.troubleshooting: On a fresh environment Django may not yet be installed; install a reviewed supported patch release only after confirming the compatible Python version.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First identify the input and the responsible Django component. Next trace how the example moves through “Installing Django” and the related concept “Installing Django with pip”. Predict the result before running or inspecting it. Finally compare the observed behavior with the expected result and the cited official documentation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to Installing Django with pip. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to describe installing django, explain the listed topics, inspect the example, and choose an appropriate verification step. Keep the scope and version caveat visible when sharing your solution.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a framework fragment without its imports, configuration, model, or URL context.
common_mistakes.why: The snippet may be incomplete when separated from a Django project.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the stated prerequisites and run the relevant management check or focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting input or relying only on a happy-path example.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid values, unauthorized requests, or concurrent activity can violate assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and add a negative or boundary test.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating the development sample as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Production hosting, secrets, storage, monitoring and resource limits differ from local use.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the current deployment/security references and document untested areas.
